claims.source: Instead, the sporadic form of CCM has relatively high prevalence, of about 1:200, and in the majority of cases, it occurs as a single cavernoma.
claims.evidence: This statement provides epidemiological data about sporadic CCM.

claims.claim: Sporadic CCM occurs as a single cavernoma in the majority of cases.
claims.source: Instead, the sporadic form of CCM has relatively high prevalence, of about 1:200, and in the majority of cases, it occurs as a single cavernoma.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on established clinical knowledge about sporadic CCM.

claims.claim: Sporadic CCM can result in symptoms similar to familial CCM that depend on cavernoma location.
claims.source: Sporadic CCM can also result in a relatively variable set of symptoms, which are similar to familial CCM and depend on the location of the cavernoma (Labauge et al., 2007; Akers et al., 2017; Cavalcanti et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: There is currently no effective pharmacological treatment for CCM patients.
claims.source: At present, to limit disease progression, there remains the need for an effective pharmacological treatment for patients with CCM, as to date, the only curative therapy is lesion eradication by surgical intervention or stereotactic radiosurgery.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on current clinical knowledge about CCM treatment options.

claims.claim: The only curative therapy for CCM is lesion eradication by surgical intervention or stereotactic radiosurgery.
claims.source: At present, to limit disease progression, there remains the need for an effective pharmacological treatment for patients with CCM, as to date, the only curative therapy is lesion eradication by surgical intervention or stereotactic radiosurgery.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on current clinical knowledge about CCM treatment.

claims.claim: Open skull surgery is currently applied to selected symptomatic CCM lesions only because it is highly invasive and can result in significant complications.
claims.source: Open skull surgery is currently applied to selected symptomatic lesions only, as it is highly invasive, and it can result in significant complications, while being accompanied by unproven long-term benefit.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on current clinical knowledge about CCM surgical treatment.

claims.claim: In familial CCM, neither surgery nor radiotherapy can cure multiple lesions throughout the brain and spinal cord.
claims.source: Also, in familial CCM, neither surgery nor radiotherapy can cure multiple lesions throughout the brain and spinal cord.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on current clinical knowledge about familial CCM treatment limitations.

claims.claim: An effective pharmacological therapy for CCM is still missing despite many studies.
claims.source: Therefore, despite many studies into CCM, an effective pharmacological therapy for this disease is still missing (Abdelilah-Seyfried et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Cdh5(PAC)-Cre-ERT2/Ccm3f/f/Cldn5(BAC)-GFP mice were used for endothelial cell-specific recombination.
claims.source: To study the EC subpopulation(s) that form lesions in CCM, we used Cdh5(PAC)-Cre-ERT2/Ccm3f/f/Cldn5(BAC)-GFP mice for EC-specific recombination (Wang et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement describes the experimental mouse model used in the study.

claims.claim: Following a single tamoxifen injection at P1, Cdh5(PAC)-Cre-ERT2/Ccm3f/f/Cldn5(BAC)-GFP mice develop CCM lesions in the brain by P8 that resemble human cavernomas.
claims.source: Following a single tamoxifen injection administered to the pups on their first day after birth, by P8 these mice develop CCM lesions in the brain that resemble human cavernomas (Figure 1A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data and images showing CCM lesion development.

claims.claim: Endothelial cells were isolated and enriched (CD45- and CD31+) from brains of both Pdcd10-wt and Pdcd10-ko littermates for droplet-based scRNA-seq.
claims.source: ECs were isolated and enriched (CD45- and CD31+) from the brain of both Cre-negative (Pdcd10-wt) and Cre-positive (Pdcd10-ko) littermates and processed for droplet-based scRNA-seq.
claims.evidence: This statement describes the experimental methods used for cell isolation and sequencing.

claims.claim: ScRNA-seq libraries were prepared using the 10× Genomics platform.
claims.source: ScRNA-seq libraries were prepared using the 10× Genomics platform, and the R toolkit Seurat (version 3) (see Materials and methods) was used for integrated data analysis (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This statement describes the experimental methods used for library preparation.

claims.claim: The R toolkit Seurat (version 3) was used for integrated data analysis.
claims.source: ScRNA-seq libraries were prepared using the 10× Genomics platform, and the R toolkit Seurat (version 3) (see Materials and methods) was used for integrated data analysis (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This statement describes the computational methods used for data analysis.

claims.claim: After quality control, 15,057 cells from two Pdcd10-wt mice and 17,204 cells from two Pdcd10-ko mice were analyzed jointly.
claims.source: After quality control, 15,057 cells from two Pdcd10-wt mice and 17,204 cells from two Pdcd10-ko mice were analyzed jointly.
claims.evidence: This statement provides quantitative data about the number of cells analyzed.

claims.claim: Through unsupervised clustering, 17 cell clusters were distinguished and visualized using UMAP.
claims.source: Through unsupervised clustering, 17 cell clusters (C) were distinguished and visualized using 'uniform manifold approximation and projection' (UMAP) (Figure 1D–F).
claims.evidence: This statement describes the results of the clustering analysis, supported by figures.

claims.claim: Four clusters were identified as mixed with non-endothelial cells (C10, C11, C15, C16).
claims.source: Based on the expression of a panel of known brain endothelial marker genes (Figure 1G; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), four clusters were identified as mixed with non-ECs (C10, C11, C15, C16).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on analysis of marker gene expression patterns shown in figures.

claims.claim: Two clusters were identified as enriched in pericytes (C11) and microglia (C16).
claims.source: While the identity of C15 remains unclear, two clusters were identified as enriched in pericytes (C11) and microglia (C16) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on analysis of marker gene expression patterns.

claims.claim: Cluster 10 appeared to be a mixture of endothelial cells and astrocytes.
claims.source: Cluster 10 (C10), instead, appeared to be a mixture of ECs and astrocytes, as marker genes of both of these cell types were highly expressed in this population (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on analysis of marker gene expression patterns.

claims.claim: The remaining 13 endothelial subpopulations were categorized into six groups: venous, arterial, capillary, tip, mitotic/capillary, and tip/capillary cells.
claims.source: The remaining 13 endothelial subpopulations were then characterized on the basis of the overall expression levels of the reported endothelial marker genes (Figure 1H,I; Supplementary file 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2E). These were categorized into six groups of ECs, as venous (C9), arterial (C8), capillary (C0, C3, C4, C5), tip (C1, C6), mitotic/capillary (C2, C7), and tip/capillary (C12, C13, C14) cells (Figure 1H,J).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on analysis of marker gene expression patterns shown in figures.

claims.claim: Capillary endothelial cells were further distinguished into venous (C2, C4, C7) and arterial (C3, C5) subtypes.
claims.source: The capillary ECs were further distinguished into venous (C2, C4, C7) and arterial (C3, C5) (Figure 1I,J; Sabbagh et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on analysis of marker gene expression patterns and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: All endothelial subpopulations except C13 showed significant down-regulation of Pdcd10 expression after Pdcd10 deletion.
claims.source: All of the endothelial subpopulations except C13 showed significant down-regulation of Pdcd10 expression after Pdcd10 deletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on analysis of gene expression data shown in a figure.

claims.claim: The mixed endothelial and non-endothelial cell clusters (C10, C11, C15, C16) did not show Pdcd10 down-regulation.
claims.source: As expected, the mixed endothelial and non-EC clusters (C10, C11, C15, C16) did not show Pdcd10 down-regulation.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on analysis of gene expression data.

claims.claim: Venous/venous capillary endothelial cells in C9 were highly modified by Pdcd10 deletion.
claims.source: The comparisons between the total numbers of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) indicated that the venous/venous capillary ECs in C9 were highly modified by Pdcd10 deletion, while the arterial ECs in C8 were essentially not affected (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Arterial endothelial cells in C8 were essentially not affected by Pdcd10 deletion.
claims.source: The comparisons between the total numbers of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) indicated that the venous/venous capillary ECs in C9 were highly modified by Pdcd10 deletion, while the arterial ECs in C8 were essentially not affected (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Arterial-capillary endothelial cells of C3 and C5 were minimally affected by Pdcd10 deletion.
claims.source: Also, the arterial- capillary ECs of C3 and C5 were minimally affected by Pdcd10 deletion (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Tip cell clusters C1 and C6 and mitotic/venous capillary C7 and capillary C0 Pdcd10-ko endothelial cell clusters showed strong modifications to their gene expression.
claims.source: Furthermore, this analysis also showed that the tip cell C1 and C6 and the mitotic/venous capillary C7 and capillary C0 Pdcd10-ko EC clusters showed strong modifications to their gene expression, which indicated that Pdcd10 deletion was particularly significant in these cells, as compared to the other cell clusters.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on differential gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: Klf4 and Klf2 are key drivers of the Pdcd10-ko phenotype and are up-regulated in brain endothelial cells after Pdcd10 deletion.
claims.source: The transcription factors Klf4 and Klf2 are key drivers of the Pdcd10-ko phenotype, and they are up-regulated in brain ECs after Pdcd10 deletion (Maddaluno et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2016; Cuttano et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Both Klf4 and Klf2 were up-regulated in Pdcd10-ko endothelial cells compared to Pdcd10-wt endothelial cells in almost all clusters (C0-C7, C9).
claims.source: Here, both Klf4 and Klf2 were up-regulated in the Pdcd10-ko ECs compared to the Pdcd10-wt ECs in almost all of the clusters (C0–C7, C9).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: Arterial C8 endothelial cells were not affected by Pdcd10 deletion in terms of Klf4 and Klf2 expression.
claims.source: The exceptions here were the arterial C8 ECs, which were not affected (further commented below), and the tip/capillary C12 and C14 ECs, which showed significant up-regulation of only Klf2 (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Tip/capillary C12 and C14 endothelial cells showed significant up-regulation of only Klf2 after Pdcd10 deletion.
claims.source: The exceptions here were the arterial C8 ECs, which were not affected (further commented below), and the tip/capillary C12 and C14 ECs, which showed significant up-regulation of only Klf2 (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: The greatest up-regulation of Klf4 and Klf2 was seen for tip cell clusters C1 and C6.
claims.source: The greatest up-regulation of Klf4 and Klf2 was seen for the tip cell clusters C1 and C6.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: Pdcd10-wt arterial endothelial cells of C8 showed significantly higher expression of Klf4 and Klf2 compared with Pdcd10-wt endothelial cells of all other clusters.
claims.source: Pdcd10-wt arterial ECs of C8 showed significantly higher expression of Klf4 and Klf2 compared with Pdcd10-wt ECs of all the other clusters (average logFC, 0.72, 0.55, respectively; padj <0.05 for both), and there were no differences in Klf4 or Klf2 expression between the Pdcd10-wt and Pdcd10-ko ECs.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis with statistical significance.

claims.claim: There were no differences in Klf4 or Klf2 expression between Pdcd10-wt and Pdcd10-ko arterial C8 endothelial cells.
claims.source: Pdcd10-wt arterial ECs of C8 showed significantly higher expression of Klf4 and Klf2 compared with Pdcd10-wt ECs of all the other clusters (average logFC, 0.72, 0.55, respectively; padj <0.05 for both), and there were no differences in Klf4 or Klf2 expression between the Pdcd10-wt and Pdcd10-ko ECs.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: Pdcd10-ko venous/venous capillary C9 endothelial cells showed up-regulation of most lesion-marker genes.
claims.source: For the Pdcd10-ko, the venous/venous capillary C9 ECs showed up-regulation of most of the lesion-marker genes, followed by the mitotic/venous capillary C7 and tip cell C1 and C6 ECs.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis of lesion markers.

claims.claim: Differentially expressed genes from cluster C9 showed the greatest overlap with the CCM gene set (12 of 51 CCM genes).
claims.source: Here, the DEGs from cluster C9 showed the greatest overlap with the CCM gene set (12 of 51 CCM genes) (Figure 2D; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on enrichment analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: The venous/venous capillary C9 endothelial cell cluster is the strongest candidate cell cluster for contributions to the most advanced lesion development after Pdcd10 deletion.
claims.source: Once again, these observations strongly support the hypothesis that the venous/venous capillary C9 EC cluster is the strongest candidate cell cluster for contributions to the most advanced lesion development after Pdcd10 deletion.
claims.evidence: This statement is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence from gene expression and enrichment analyses.

claims.claim: In the absence of Pdcd10 in venous/venous capillary C9 and tip cell C1 and C6 endothelial cells, biological processes implicated in CCM pathology were mainly altered, including angiogenesis, cell differentiation, coagulation, immune responses, and cell apoptosis.
claims.source: In the absence of Pdcd10 in the venous/venous capillary C9 and tip cell C1 and C6 ECs, the biological processes implicated in CCM pathology were mainly altered, which included angiogenesis, cell differentiation, coagulation, immune responses, and cell apoptosis (Figure 2E; Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene set enrichment analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Endothelial cells undergo endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition mediated through increased TGFβ signaling in CCM.
claims.source: In a previous study, we reported that ECs undergo endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition that is mediated through increased TGFβ signaling (Maddaluno et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research by the authors.

claims.claim: Endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition is relevant for the development of vascular lesions in CCM.
claims.source: This process is relevant for the development of vascular lesions, and is further confirmed here by this single-cell analysis (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on the current single-cell analysis data.

claims.claim: In patients with CCM, the blood-brain barrier is impaired.
claims.source: In patients with CCM, the BBB is impaired (Clatterbuck, 2001; Mikati et al., 2015), as reported here in this murine Pdcd10-depletion model, where there was significant increase in vascular permeability to endogenous immunoglobulins (Figure 2F, cerebellum; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, cerebrum).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research and confirmed by experimental data shown in figures.

claims.claim: The murine Pdcd10-depletion model showed significant increase in vascular permeability to endogenous immunoglobulins.
claims.source: In patients with CCM, the BBB is impaired (Clatterbuck, 2001; Mikati et al., 2015), as reported here in this murine Pdcd10-depletion model, where there was significant increase in vascular permeability to endogenous immunoglobulins (Figure 2F, cerebellum; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, cerebrum).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on experimental data shown in figures.

claims.claim: Expression levels of many regulators of BBB formation and maturation were decreased in the potential lesion-forming C9 and C6 clusters.
claims.source: Coherent with this, the expression levels of many regulators of BBB formation and maturation that cooperate to establish the BBB (e.g. Foxf2, Foxq1, Ppard, Zic3) (Hupe et al., 2017) were decreased in the potential lesion-forming C9 and C6 clusters (Figure 2G, pink).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis shown in a figure and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: BBB transporters were diffusely down-regulated in Pdcd10-ko cells, with C9, C6, and C7 endothelial cells as the most affected.
claims.source: Transporters that finely tune BBB functions (Figure 2G, green) were also diffusely down-regulated in the Pdcd10-ko cells, with the C9, C6, and C7 ECs as the most affected.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Three transporters (Slc2a1/Glut1, Slc9a3r2, Slc6a6) were all up-regulated in Pdcd10-ko cells of C1, C6, C7, C9, and C12 endothelial cells.
claims.source: Of note, three transporters (i.e. Slc2a1 or Glut1, Slc9a3r2, Slc6a6) were all up-regulated in the Pdcd10-ko cells of the C1, C6, C7, C9, and C12 ECs.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: Enhancement of glucose transport mediated by Slc2a1 supports glycolytic metabolism in endothelial cells of tumor vessels.
claims.source: Interestingly, enhancement of glucose transport mediated by Slc2a1 supports glycolytic metabolism in ECs of tumor vessels (Rohlenova et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Arterial C8 Pdcd10-ko endothelial cells and putative arterial-capillary C3 and C5 endothelial cells were minimally or not modified by Pdcd10 deletion.
claims.source: All of these functions indicated were minimally or not modified in the arterial C8 Pdcd10-ko ECs (Figure 2A–G) and in the putative arterial-capillary C3 and C5 ECs (Figure 1J), which were only partially affected by the Pdcd10 deletion (Figure 2A–G).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: Only Cldn5 expression was down-regulated in C1, C6, and C9 endothelial cells among junctional molecules investigated.
claims.source: Among the panel of junctional molecules investigated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), only Cldn5 expression was down-regulated in the C1, C6, and C9 ECs.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Little or no changes were seen for the expression of other adherens and tight-junction components in Pdcd10-ko endothelial cells.
claims.source: Little or no changes were seen for the expression of other adherens and tight-junction components (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Tight-junction proteins Claudin-5 and Cingulin, as well as adherens junction VE-cadherin, were not correctly localized at cell-to-cell contacts in endothelial cells of cavernomas in Pdcd10-ko mice.
claims.source: However, the tight-junction proteins Claudin-5, and Cingulin, as well as the adherens junction VE-cadherin were not correctly localized at the cell-to-cell contacts in the ECs of the cavernomas of the Pdcd10-ko mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on immunofluorescence data shown in figures.

claims.claim: Four endothelial subpopulations are particularly affected by Pdcd10 gene deletion: venous/venous capillary C9, tip cell C1 and C6, and mitotic/venous capillary C7 endothelial cell clusters.
claims.source: In summary here, we have identified four endothelial subpopulations that are particularly affected by the deletion of the Pdcd10 gene: the venous/venous capillary C9, tip cell C1 and C6, and mitotic/venous capillary C7 EC clusters.
claims.evidence: This statement is a summary inference based on multiple lines of evidence from gene expression analyses.

claims.claim: Under Pdcd10-ko conditions, venous/venous capillary C9 endothelial cells represent the strongest candidate to form the most advanced lesions or most progressed lesion areas.
claims.source: Among these, under the Pdcd10-ko conditions here, the venous/venous capillary C9 ECs represent the strongest candidate to form the most advanced lesions, or the most progressed lesion areas.
claims.evidence: This statement is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence from gene expression analyses.

claims.claim: The venous nature of endothelial cells in cavernomas was confirmed by expression of the venous marker COUP-TFII in vivo in CCM lesions.
claims.source: The venous nature of the ECs in the cavernomas was further confirmed by expression of the venous marker COUP-TFII in vivo in the CCM lesions. Figure 2H shows the ECs in a large cavernoma that can be seen to be strongly positive for the venous marker COUP-TFII, which is encoded by Nr2f2.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on immunofluorescence data shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Endothelial cells in a large cavernoma are strongly positive for the venous marker COUP-TFII (encoded by Nr2f2).
claims.source: Figure 2H shows the ECs in a large cavernoma that can be seen to be strongly positive for the venous marker COUP-TFII, which is encoded by Nr2f2.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on immunofluorescence data shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Despite successful deletion of the Pdcd10 gene, gene expression of arterial endothelial cells (C8) in Pdcd10-ko mice was almost unchanged from the effects of Pdcd10 deletion.
claims.source: Despite the successful deletion of the Pdcd10 gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), gene expression of the arterial ECs (C8) in the Pdcd10-ko mice was almost unchanged from the effects of Pdcd10 deletion.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Arterial C8 endothelial cells showed the lowest total number of differentially expressed genes in comparison of Pdcd10-wt and Pdcd10-ko mice.
claims.source: Indeed, in the comparison of the Pdcd10-wt and Pdcd10-ko mice, these arterial ECs showed the following: the lowest total number of DEGs (Figure 2A); no increase in Klf4 and Klf2 expression (Figure 2B); no, or minimal, signs of increased expression of lesion markers (Figure 2C–E); and no, or minimal, decreases in BBB markers and BBB transporters (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in figures.

claims.claim: 111 unique marker genes were identified for the arterial C8 cluster with specificity average logFC >0.25 and padj <0.05.
claims.source: Therefore, to investigate the features of these arterial ECs that might promote their refractoriness to lesion formation, we identified the unique marker genes that were expressed in this C8 cluster (threshold: specificity average logFC >0.25; padj <0.05) (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis with specified statistical thresholds.

claims.claim: Out of 111 unique marker genes highly expressed in C8 endothelial cell cluster, 80 had potential preventive functions, 5 had potential promotive functions, and 13 had potential dual functions.
claims.source: Out of a total of 111 unique marker genes that were highly expressed in the C8 EC cluster, 80 had potential preventive functions, five had potential promotive functions, and 13 had potential dual functions, which depended on the cellular context (Figure 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on functional annotation of unique marker genes shown in figures.

claims.claim: Four regulators of DNA remodeling (Chd3, Gadd45g, Hey1, Mapk3) and 10 transcriptional factors were uniquely up-regulated in arterial C8 endothelial cells.
claims.source: These specific functions of the C8 cluster might also be supported by the group of four regulators of DNA remodeling (i.e. Chd3, Gadd45g, Hey1, Mapk3) and 10 transcriptional factors (Gata2, Lmo7, Mecom, Msx1, Notch1, Notch4, Smad7, Sox13, Sox17, Sox18) that were uniquely up-regulated in these arterial C8 ECs (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: The levels of expression of Klf2 and Klf4 do not directly correlate with resistance to Pdcd10 deletion.
claims.source: Notably, the levels of expression of Klf2 and Klf4 do not directly correlate with the resistance to Pdcd10 deletion.
claims.evidence: This statement is an inference based on the observation that arterial C8 cells have high Klf2/Klf4 but are resistant to Pdcd10 deletion.

claims.claim: High levels of Klf2/Klf4 are not sufficient per se to trigger the Pdcd10 phenotype.
claims.source: This suggests that high levels of Klf2/Klf4 are not sufficient per se to trigger the Pdcd10 phenotype.
claims.evidence: This statement is an inference based on the observation that arterial C8 cells have high Klf2/Klf4 but do not develop the Pdcd10 phenotype.

claims.claim: Arterial endothelial cells selectively express genes that positively regulate processes altered after Pdcd10 deletion.
claims.source: Taken together, it appears that these arterial ECs selectively express genes that positively regulate processes that are altered after the Pdcd10 deletion.
claims.evidence: This statement is an inference based on the functional annotation of unique marker genes in arterial C8 cells.

claims.claim: Genes expressed in arterial endothelial cells can counteract the effects of Pdcd10 deletion and prevent lesion formation.
claims.source: We hypothesize that these genes can counteract the effects of the Pdcd10 deletion, and thus prevent lesion formation.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that arterial cells express putative preventive genes and are resistant to lesion formation.

claims.claim: The number of Pdcd10-ko cells was significantly increased over respective Pdcd10-wt cells for C9 (4.8-fold), C12 (4.0-fold), and C14 (2.8-fold).
claims.source: The number of Pdcd10-ko cells was significantly increased over the respective Pdcd10-wt cells for C9 (4.8-fold), C12 (4.0-fold), and C14 (2.8-fold) (Figure 1E,F; Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of cell numbers shown in figures.

claims.claim: Cluster 9 enrichment in Pdcd10-ko cells is likely due to sustained proliferation.
claims.source: Cluster nine enrichment in the Pdcd10-ko cells is likely due to sustained proliferation, as indicated by the greater proportion of the Pdcd10-ko cells (vs. Pdcd10-wt) that expressed mitotic markers (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This statement is an inference based on analysis of mitotic marker expression shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Pdcd10-ko cells of C9 expressed significantly higher levels of several mitotic markers that regulate different phases of mitosis.
claims.source: Furthermore, Pdcd10-ko cells of C9 expressed significantly higher levels of several mitotic markers that regulate different phases of mitosis (Figure 4C), including: G2/M (Ccnb2); mitotic spindle orientation (Cenpa); sister chromatid segregation (Top2a); and exit from mitosis (Ube2s, Ube2c, Birc5) (see references in Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis shown in a figure and supported by references.

claims.claim: Increased numbers of mitotic endothelial cells (co-expressing Ki-67 and ERG) were seen in cavernomas but not in pseudo-normal vessels of Pdcd10-ko brain.
claims.source: Accordingly, increased numbers of mitotic ECs (i.e. co-expression of Ki-67 and ERG Birdsey et al., 2015; Booth and Earnshaw, 2017) were seen for cavernomas, but not in the pseudo-normal vessels of the Pdcd10-ko brain (Figure 4D, representative immunofluorescence; Figure 4E, quantification; Video 1).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in figures and video, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Visium analysis confirmed enhanced proliferation specifically in endothelial cells of cavernomas.
claims.source: This analysis of the Visium data confirmed enhanced proliferation specifically in the ECs of the cavernomas (Figure 4F,G).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on spatial transcriptomics data shown in figures.

claims.claim: Increased proportions of Pdcd10-ko cells expressed tip cell markers (Plaur, Apln, Mmrn2) in C9 and Plaur in C12.
claims.source: For the tip cell traits, as the other crucial phenotype in angiogenesis, increased proportions of the Pdcd10-ko cells expressed a set of tip cell markers in C9 (i.e. Plaur, Apln, Mmrn2) and C12 (i.e. Plaur) (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Tip cell clusters C1 and C6 showed the greatest number of up-regulated tip cell markers.
claims.source: While tip cell clusters C1 and C6 showed the greatest number of up-regulated tip cell markers (Figure 5B), C9 Pdcd10-ko cells showed up-regulated expression of only a few tip cell markers (Figure 5B, Mcam, Apln, Plaur).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis shown in a figure.

claims.claim: C9 Pdcd10-ko cells showed up-regulation of a large set of tumor tip cell markers, which were less modified in C1 and C6.
claims.source: Conversely, C9 Pdcd10-ko cells showed up-regulation of a large set of tumor tip cell markers (Zhao et al., 2018), which were less modified in C1 and C6 (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on gene expression analysis shown in a figure and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: uPAR (encoded by Plaur) was highly expressed in both overt lesions and pseudo-normal vessels of brains from Pdcd10-ko mice.
claims.source: According to the enhanced expression of the tip cell marker Plaur in the Pdcd10-ko cells of C9 (as well as in various other clusters), uPAR (encoded by Plaur) was highly expressed both in overt lesions and in pseudo-normal vessels of the brains from the Pdcd10-ko mice, as shown in Figure 5D, and quantified in Figure 5E.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in figures.

claims.claim: The densities of tip cells were similar in Pdcd10-wt and Pdcd10-ko brains when considering both pseudo-normal vessels and cavernomas.
claims.source: However, considering both pseudo-normal vessels and cavernomas, the densities of the tip cells were similar in the Pdcd10-wt and Pdcd10-ko brains (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on quantification of tip cells shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Tip cells at the vascular front were significantly denser in retinas from Pdcd10-ko than Pdcd10-wt.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM), describing it as a rare neurovascular disease characterized by enlarged and irregular blood vessels leading to cerebral hemorrhage. CCM occurs in familial and sporadic forms, with familial CCM caused by loss-of-function mutations in KRIT1, CCM2, or PDCD10 genes. Current treatment is limited to surgical intervention or stereotactic radiosurgery, with no effective pharmacological therapy available.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1, C2, C17-C31) represent well-established background knowledge about CCM disease, supported by multiple citations to previous research and clinical knowledge. The epidemiological data, genetic basis, clinical manifestations, and treatment limitations are consistent with the scientific literature on CCM.

results.result: This study reports the first in-depth single-cell RNA sequencing combined with spatial transcriptomics and immunohistochemistry to characterize brain endothelial cell subclasses in CCM. The authors used Cdh5(PAC)-Cre-ERT2/Ccm3f/f/Cldn5(BAC)-GFP mice that develop CCM lesions by P8 following tamoxifen injection at P1. Endothelial cells were isolated (CD45- and CD31+) from brains of Pdcd10-wt and Pdcd10-ko littermates, and 32,261 cells were analyzed using 10× Genomics platform and Seurat (version 3).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C32-C37 describe the experimental approach and are well-supported by the methods section and data presented. The novelty claim (C3) is reasonable given the integration of multiple technologies. Sample sizes (n=2 mice per condition, >30,000 cells total) are adequate for scRNA-seq studies, and the methods are clearly described with appropriate tools and versions specified.

results.result: Through unsupervised clustering, 17 cell clusters were identified and visualized using UMAP. Four clusters (C10, C11, C15, C16) were identified as mixed with non-endothelial cells, including pericytes (C11), microglia (C16), and astrocytes (C10). The remaining 13 endothelial subpopulations were categorized into six groups: venous (C9), arterial (C8), capillary (C0, C3, C4, C5), tip (C1, C6), mitotic/capillary (C2, C7), and tip/capillary (C12, C13, C14) cells. All endothelial subpopulations except C13 showed significant down-regulation of Pdcd10 expression after deletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C45 describe the clustering results and cell type identification, which are supported by Figure 1 and supplementary data. The cluster annotations are based on established marker genes (Supplementary file 1) and appear consistent with known endothelial cell biology. The confirmation of Pdcd10 deletion in most clusters validates the experimental model. However, the identity of C15 remains unclear (C39), which is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Differential gene expression analysis revealed that venous/venous capillary ECs in C9 were highly modified by Pdcd10 deletion, while arterial ECs in C8 were essentially not affected. Tip cell clusters C1 and C6, mitotic/venous capillary C7, and capillary C0 showed strong modifications. Klf4 and Klf2, key drivers of the Pdcd10-ko phenotype, were up-regulated in almost all clusters except arterial C8. Notably, Pdcd10-wt arterial C8 ECs showed significantly higher baseline expression of Klf4 and Klf2 compared to other clusters, with no differences between Pdcd10-wt and Pdcd10-ko.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C56 are well-supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2A-B and referenced supplementary files. The statistical thresholds (padj <0.05) are appropriate. The observation that arterial C8 cells have high baseline Klf2/Klf4 but are resistant to Pdcd10 deletion is particularly interesting and well-documented. The data support the conclusion that Klf2/Klf4 upregulation alone is insufficient for the mutant phenotype.

results.result: Pdcd10-ko venous/venous capillary C9 ECs showed up-regulation of most lesion-marker genes and the greatest overlap with the CCM gene set (12 of 51 CCM genes). Gene set enrichment analysis revealed that biological processes implicated in CCM pathology were mainly altered in C9 and tip cell C1 and C6 ECs, including angiogenesis, cell differentiation, coagulation, immune responses, and cell apoptosis. Endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition mediated through increased TGFβ signaling was confirmed.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C62 are supported by gene expression analysis (Figure 2C-E) and enrichment analysis using EnrichR and GSEA. The overlap with known CCM genes (C58) provides validation. The confirmation of endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (C61-C62) is supported by both current data and previous work by the authors (Maddaluno et al., 2013). The statistical methods and thresholds are appropriate.

results.result: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is impaired in CCM, as demonstrated by significant increase in vascular permeability to endogenous immunoglobulins in the Pdcd10-depletion model. Expression levels of BBB formation and maturation regulators were decreased in C9 and C6 clusters, and BBB transporters were diffusely down-regulated in Pdcd10-ko cells. While gene expression of most junctional molecules was unchanged, tight-junction proteins (Claudin-5, Cingulin) and adherens junction VE-cadherin were not correctly localized at cell-to-cell contacts in cavernomas.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C72 are well-supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), gene expression analysis (Figure 2G), and citations to previous research. The distinction between gene expression (mostly unchanged, C70-C71) and protein localization (disrupted, C72) is important and well-documented. The quantification of IgG leakage (C64) provides functional validation of BBB impairment with appropriate statistics (n=6-7, p<0.01).

results.result: Four endothelial subpopulations are particularly affected by Pdcd10 deletion: venous/venous capillary C9, tip cell C1 and C6, and mitotic/venous capillary C7. Among these, C9 ECs represent the strongest candidate to form the most advanced lesions. The venous nature of cavernomas was confirmed by expression of the venous marker COUP-TFII (encoded by Nr2f2) in vivo in CCM lesions.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 represent a synthesis of multiple lines of evidence from differential gene expression, lesion marker analysis, and CCM gene enrichment. The conclusion is well-supported by the data presented in Figures 1-2. The immunofluorescence confirmation of COUP-TFII expression in cavernomas (C75-C76, Figure 2H) provides important validation of the venous identity at the protein level.

results.result: Arterial endothelial cells (C8) are refractory to CCM transformation. Despite successful Pdcd10 deletion, arterial C8 ECs showed minimal gene expression changes, with the lowest number of differentially expressed genes, no increase in Klf4/Klf2, and minimal changes in lesion markers or BBB markers. Analysis of 111 unique marker genes in C8 revealed that 80 had potential preventive functions. The authors hypothesize that these genes can counteract the effects of Pdcd10 deletion and prevent lesion formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C77-C85 are well-supported by comprehensive gene expression analysis (Figures 2-3). The identification of unique marker genes with potential preventive functions (C79-C80) is based on appropriate statistical thresholds (logFC >0.25, padj <0.05) and manual annotation using established databases. The observation that high Klf2/Klf4 levels are not sufficient for the mutant phenotype (C82-C83) is an important mechanistic insight. However, the hypothesis about preventive gene function (C85) requires experimental validation.

results.result: The number of Pdcd10-ko cells was significantly increased in C9 (4.8-fold), C12 (4.0-fold), and C14 (2.8-fold). C9 enrichment is likely due to sustained proliferation, as indicated by increased expression of mitotic markers and higher proportions of cells expressing mitotic markers. Increased numbers of mitotic ECs (co-expressing Ki-67 and ERG) were observed in cavernomas but not in pseudo-normal vessels, confirmed by both immunofluorescence and Visium spatial transcriptomics.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90 are well-supported by multiple complementary approaches: scRNA-seq cell counts (Figure 4A), mitotic marker expression analysis (Figure 4B-C), immunofluorescence with quantification (Figure 4D-E, n=6 per group, p<0.01), and spatial transcriptomics validation (Figure 4F-G). The convergence of evidence from different methodologies strengthens the conclusion about increased proliferation in C9 cells.

results.result: Increased proportions of Pdcd10-ko cells expressed tip cell markers in C9 and C12. While tip cell clusters C1 and C6 showed the greatest number of up-regulated tip cell markers, C9 Pdcd10-ko cells showed up-regulation of tumor tip cell markers. In retinas, tip cells at the vascular front were significantly denser in Pdcd10-ko, but 15-30% appeared blocked within the dense cell layer (tip-like cells) compared to 10% in Pdcd10-wt. Radial expansion of the vascular network was significantly inhibited in Pdcd10-ko retina.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C101 are supported by gene expression analysis (Figure 5A-C), immunofluorescence (Figure 5D-F), and quantification in both brain (n=6 per group) and retina (n=10-13 per group) with appropriate statistics. The distinction between normal tip cells and blocked 'tip-like' cells (C98-C99) is an important observation supported by morphological analysis. The impaired radial expansion (C100) provides functional validation of the defective tip cell phenotype.

results.result: Pdcd10-ko cells of C9 are more mitotic than Pdcd10-wt cells and express tip cell traits, although with an abnormal profile. Visium analysis confirmed that 15-30% of lesion EC spots were positive for both tip cell and mitotic markers. The angiogenic phenotype is defective, with impaired network elongation and enhanced cell proliferation. The combination of high cell proliferation and low cell motility might explain cavernoma formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C107 represent a synthesis of the proliferation and tip cell data. The conclusion is well-supported by convergent evidence from scRNA-seq, immunofluorescence, and spatial transcriptomics. The mechanistic hypothesis about cavernoma formation (C107) is reasonable and supported by a citation (Castro et al., 2019), though it remains speculative and would benefit from direct experimental testing.

results.result: STREAM trajectory analysis revealed that Pdcd10-ko cells of C9 were distributed over different branches (S3-S0, S0-S2, S0-S1). Cells in the S0-S2 branch highly expressed typical cavernoma markers, were mainly mitotic, and had pathological tip cell traits, representing ECs of typical cavernoma lesions. These cells showed increased expression of Tcf15 and Id1, with Id1 inhibiting Tcf15-mediated progenitor cell differentiation but not proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C114 are supported by trajectory analysis using STREAM (Figure 6) and differential gene expression analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A). The computational approach is appropriate and well-described. The interpretation regarding Id1 and Tcf15 function (C114) is supported by citation to Davies et al., 2013. The trajectory analysis provides important insights into the developmental progression of lesion formation.

results.result: Cavernomas have clonal origins from expansion of Pdcd10-ko progenitor cells. The proportions of Pdcd10-ko cells positive for Bst1 or Peg3 were highly increased in the S0-S2 and S3-S0 branches, while Procr and Cd200 were similar across branches. Increased proportions of Mki67-positive Pdcd10-ko progenitor cells were observed in all branches, with strongest increases in S0-S2. Klf4 and Klf2 were highly expressed in Pdcd10-ko progenitor cells, supporting the concept that they are early response genes to Pdcd10 deletion in resident endothelial progenitor cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C124 are supported by trajectory analysis (Figure 6E-G) and previous work by the authors (Malinverno et al., 2019). The analysis of progenitor marker expression across trajectory branches is methodologically sound, with appropriate thresholds (Q1 for positive cells). The observation that Klf4/Klf2 are highly expressed in progenitor cells (C123-C124) provides important mechanistic insight into early responses to Pdcd10 deletion.

results.result: Spatial transcriptomics and in-situ hybridization confirmed concentration of Bst1 progenitor cell transcripts at cavernomas and mulberry lesions. After Pdcd10 deletion, proportions of Bst1-positive cells increased in all capillary-vein clusters (C2, C4, C7), with greatest expression in venous C9 (39.9%), but did not increase in arterial C8 or arterial capillary C3 and C5. Bst1 appears to be a preferential marker of vein-resident progenitor cells. Peg3 showed highest expression in venous C9 Pdcd10-ko cells (24.0% vs. 9.3% in wt), while Procr and Cd200 were ubiquitously expressed and did not significantly increase after Pdcd10 deletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C133 are well-supported by multiple complementary approaches: Visium spatial transcriptomics (Figure 7A-B), in-situ hybridization (Figure 7C), and scRNA-seq analysis (Figure 7D). The differential expression of progenitor markers between venous and arterial clusters (C127-C129) is an important finding that aligns with the overall conclusion about venous origin of lesions. Sample sizes for Visium (n=2 per genotype) and in-situ hybridization (n=3 per genotype) are adequate.

results.result: This study identifies venous endothelial cell clusters and their related progenitor cells as the main cell types responsible for cavernoma development. Brain ECs represent a heterogeneous population distributed across 13 clusters expressing highly specialized functions. Resident progenitor cells were detected in all Pdcd10-wt clusters in different proportions and are heterogeneous, sharing transcriptional features with ECs of the vessels where they reside. Although Pdcd10 deletion occurs comparably in arterial and venous ECs, only venous ECs respond, following defective differentiation and angiogenic programs with abnormal tip cell traits and increased mitosis. While Klf2 and Klf4 are necessary for the mutant phenotype, they are not sufficient; a specific transcriptional landscape appears necessary for full transformation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C134-C147 represent the major conclusions of the study, synthesizing evidence from scRNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, immunohistochemistry, and trajectory analysis. The conclusions are well-supported by the comprehensive dataset. The observation that Klf2/Klf4 are necessary but not sufficient (C145) is an important mechanistic insight supported by the arterial C8 data. The speculation about progenitor cell identity (C138) is appropriately presented as speculative. The overall conclusion about venous origin of lesions (C147) is strongly supported by convergent evidence.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on endothelial cell heterogeneity and specialization, describing how ECs of arteries, veins, and lymphatic system show high degrees of specialization. Brain microcirculation ECs regulate cerebral blood flow, oxygen delivery, and supply of energy metabolites. These cells form the blood-brain barrier (BBB) in neurovascular units, where ECs are surrounded by pericytes and in contact with glia and neurons. The BBB controls entry of neurotoxic components and promotes passage of nutrients through specialized transport systems. Several genetic pathologies causing BBB alterations arise from inactivation of specific genes in neurovascular unit cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C16 provide essential background on endothelial cell biology and BBB function, all supported by appropriate citations to previous research (Kalucka et al., 2020; Vanlandewijck et al., 2018; Augustin and Koh, 2017; Zhao et al., 2015; Armulik et al., 2010; Iadecola, 2017). This background is accurate and provides necessary context for the study.
